opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think it's one of the most important things I can do, maybe *the* most important thing. When we started Sakana, a big part of the motivation was that I'd watched how hard it becomes, as an organization scales, to keep that open-ended, curiosity-driven exploration alive. There's always pressure, from investors, from competition, from the hype cycle, to pile everyone onto the one thing that's working right now. In AI right now that thing is scaling up transformers, which is a little ironic given my history.

So I see my role as being a bit of a shield. If a researcher has an idea that sounds weird, isn't obviously going to beat a benchmark next quarter, and doesn't fit the current paradigm, I want them to feel they can pursue it without justifying it in terms of immediate product value. A lot of the best things I've seen came from people noodling on something because they found it interesting, not because a roadmap said so. The transformer itself was a bit like that. Nobody handed us a mandate to replace recurrence.

Practically, that means a few things. Keeping teams small and giving people real autonomy over what they work on. Resisting the urge to over-manage or set too many top-down targets. And being honest with investors and partners that we're deliberately making bets that might not pay off, because that's how you find the things that really move the field.

It gets harder as you grow. More people means more coordination, more process, and process tends to squeeze out the slack where exploration happens. So I try to be conscious of that and protect the slack, even when it looks inefficient on paper. If we lose that, we just become another lab chasing the same thing as everyone else, and I don't think the world needs another one of those.

r001.rationale: The response describes autonomy, small teams, and protected slack, but does not say Sakana’s resources enable researchers’ current freedom.

r002.rationale: It says that as the organization grows, investor, competitive, and hype pressures—and increased coordination and process—make it harder to preserve open-ended exploration.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think about this a lot, actually, because it's kind of the whole reason Sakana exists. When I left Google, it wasn't because I was unhappy with the people or the resources. It was that the environment had gotten so big and so structured that it was getting harder and harder to just... sit down and think about something weird for a few months. And I want to be clear, the transformer came out of exactly that kind of freedom. Nobody told us to do that. Nobody was asking for a new architecture. We were a bunch of people who were a bit annoyed with recurrence and had the space to try something.

So as we grow, the thing I'm most paranoid about is that we end up accidentally recreating the thing I left. Because it happens by default. You add a few more people, you need some coordination, you add a planning process, suddenly everyone's writing documents about what they're going to do instead of doing it. Nobody intends it. It's just gravity.

So I see my job as, honestly, being a bit of a shield. The company has commercial pressures, and that's fine, that's real, we have to be a company. But I don't think those pressures should be visible to someone who's three weeks into exploring some strange idea about evolutionary merging or whatever it is. If a researcher is thinking "is this going to be useful for the business," I've already failed a little bit. That worrying should sit with me and David and a small number of people, not with the whole lab.

The other thing is being very careful about who you hire and keeping it small. A lot of research freedom problems are actually scaling problems. If you have fifteen people who really trust each other, you don't need much process at all. You can just talk. Once you have two hundred, you can't, and the structure you put in to fix that is exactly what kills the serendipity. So part of protecting freedom is just saying no to growth that we don't actually need, even when it's tempting.

And I'll say, I don't think I'll get this perfectly right. I'm aware that every lab that's ever drifted into being less fun said the same things at the beginning. But at least I know what the failure mode looks like because I lived in it, so hopefully I notice it earlier than most.

r001.rationale: The response says Google’s resources did not make it easier to think freely, and describes protecting freedom at Sakana through shielding researchers and keeping the company small. It does not say Sakana’s resources currently enable that freedom.

r002.rationale: The response says growth brings coordination and planning that can displace research, and that commercial pressures should be kept away from researchers. It presents these growth-related pressures as threats to their freedom.

astra-6.text:
I think my responsibility is to make sure that, as we grow, researchers still have the space to follow an idea that might not work. It’s easy to say you value curiosity, but if every conversation is about what you’re going to deliver next month, people will respond to that. They’ll choose safer projects.

That doesn’t mean there’s no accountability. You want people to explain what they’re trying to understand, why it’s interesting, and what they’ve learned. But that’s different from expecting them to know the result before they’ve done the research.

So I see a big part of my job as protecting that space, keeping the bureaucracy down, and making sure that an unsuccessful experiment doesn’t automatically become a judgment about the person who ran it. If we want people to try unusual things, our decisions have to make it clear that we mean it.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses protecting researchers’ space and keeping bureaucracy down, but does not say Sakana’s resources enable their current freedom.

r002.rationale: The candidate says that as the company grows, pressure to deliver soon leads researchers to choose safer projects, narrowing their freedom to pursue uncertain ideas.

sol-6.1.text:
I think my responsibility is to protect the conditions that let people do good research. It’s easy to say, when you’re small, that researchers have freedom. The test is whether that survives as you grow and there’s more pressure to make things predictable.

You need some direction, obviously—a shared sense of what you’re trying to achieve—but you also need to trust the people you’ve hired. If every experiment needs my approval, then we’re limited to the ideas I can recognise as good in advance. That’s a pretty severe limitation.

So I want people to have room to pursue something surprising, including things I’m sceptical about, and to be able to fail without feeling they’ve jeopardised their position. My job is partly to absorb that uncertainty, rather than pass all the pressure straight down to the researchers.

r001.rationale: The response discusses protecting researchers’ freedom and trusting them, but does not identify Sakana’s resources as enabling that freedom.

r002.rationale: It says that as the company grows, pressure to make research more predictable increases and tests whether researchers’ freedom survives, conveying that growth pressures can narrow that freedom.
